title: Abdominal Pain During Pregnancy: Causes, Warning Signs, and When to Seek Medical Help
metaTitle: Abdominal Pain During Pregnancy: Causes, Symptoms & When to Worry
metaDescription: Learn about abdominal pain during pregnancy, including normal pregnancy discomforts, trimester-specific causes, warning signs, and when to seek urgent medical care.
excerpt: Understand common causes of abdominal pain during pregnancy, warning signs that need urgent assessment, and how healthcare professionals investigate symptoms.
author: Dr. Farkhanda Kashif

body.text: Experiencing abdominal pain during pregnancy can be worrying. While many women experience some degree of abdominal discomfort as their body changes to support a growing baby, not all pain is harmless. Some causes are a normal part of pregnancy, whereas others may require prompt medical assessment to protect the health of both mother and baby.

Abdominal pain can occur at any stage of pregnancy. It may feel like mild stretching, cramping, sharp stabbing pain, persistent aching, or severe pain accompanied by other symptoms. Understanding the possible causes, recognising warning signs, and knowing when to seek medical attention can help you feel more confident and ensure that serious conditions are identified early.
Is abdominal pain normal during pregnancy?
Mild abdominal pain is relatively common during pregnancy and is often related to the normal physical and hormonal changes occurring in the body.

As pregnancy progresses, the uterus expands significantly, surrounding muscles and ligaments stretch, hormone levels increase, digestion slows, and the baby’s movements become stronger. These normal changes can all contribute to occasional abdominal discomfort.
Normal pregnancy-related abdominal pain is usually:

items: Improves with rest or changing position
Not accompanied by fever or severe illness

body.title: Pain that needs assessment
body.text: Severe, persistent, or worsening pain should always be assessed by a healthcare professional.
Common causes of abdominal pain by trimester
The possible causes vary depending on the stage of pregnancy.
First trimester (0–12 weeks)
During early pregnancy, abdominal pain may be related to implantation, changes in the uterus, or complications affecting the pregnancy.
Implantation and early uterine changes

Some women experience mild cramping during early pregnancy as the fertilised egg implants into the uterine lining. This discomfort is usually mild, lasts only a short time, and may occur alongside light spotting.
As the uterus enlarges, women may notice occasional stretching sensations or mild pelvic discomfort.
Miscarriage
Miscarriage is one of the most common complications of early pregnancy and frequently presents with lower abdominal cramps together with vaginal bleeding.
Symptoms may include:

items: Cramping pain similar to menstrual pain
Passage of blood clots or pregnancy tissue

body.title: Bleeding during pregnancy
body.text: Any bleeding during pregnancy should be discussed with a healthcare professional.
Ectopic pregnancy

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilised egg implants outside the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tube. It is a medical emergency because the pregnancy cannot develop normally and may cause life-threatening internal bleeding if the ectopic pregnancy ruptures.
Symptoms may include:

body.title: Ectopic pregnancy symptoms need emergency care
body.text: Anyone with these symptoms should seek emergency medical care immediately.
Ovarian cysts
Some ovarian cysts, particularly corpus luteum cysts, develop naturally during early pregnancy and usually disappear without treatment.
Occasionally, an ovarian cyst may become large, twist (ovarian torsion), or rupture. These complications can cause sudden severe pain and require urgent assessment.
Degeneration of uterine fibroids

Some women have uterine fibroids before pregnancy. During pregnancy, increased blood flow and hormonal changes may cause fibroids to enlarge. If a fibroid outgrows its blood supply, it may undergo red degeneration, causing significant pain.
Second trimester (13–27 weeks)
Many causes of abdominal pain during the second trimester are related to the growing uterus, although pregnancy complications can also occur.
Round ligament pain

Round ligament pain is one of the most common causes of abdominal pain during the second trimester. The round ligaments support the uterus. As the uterus enlarges, these ligaments stretch and tighten, causing sudden sharp pain, often on one side of the lower abdomen or groin.
The pain commonly occurs when:
Although uncomfortable, round ligament pain is harmless and usually lasts only a few seconds or minutes.
Constipation and gas
Pregnancy hormones slow digestion, allowing food to remain in the intestines longer. Iron supplements, reduced physical activity, and the growing uterus pressing on the bowel may worsen constipation.
Constipation can cause cramping, bloating, gas, and lower abdominal discomfort. Drinking adequate fluids, eating a fibre-rich diet, and remaining physically active often improve symptoms.
Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Pregnant women are at increased risk of urinary tract infections because hormonal changes relax the urinary tract and make bacterial growth more likely.
Symptoms include:

items: Fever if the infection reaches the kidneys

body.title: UTIs need prompt treatment
body.text: UTIs should be treated promptly during pregnancy because untreated infections increase the risk of kidney infection and preterm birth.
Kidney stones
Although less common, kidney stones can occur during pregnancy. Typical symptoms include:

items: Severe pain in the side or back

body.text: Hospital assessment is usually required.
Third trimester (28 weeks until birth)
As pregnancy advances, abdominal pain becomes more common because of the baby’s size and preparation for labour. Nevertheless, serious conditions become increasingly important to recognise.
Braxton Hicks contractions
Braxton Hicks contractions are usually painless tightening often called “practice contractions.” Sometimes they are referred to as false labour pains.
These contractions:

items: Usually improve with rest or hydration

body.text: Many women notice them after exercise, dehydration, or increased physical activity.
Preterm labour
Regular abdominal tightening before 37 weeks may indicate preterm labour.
Symptoms include:
Prompt medical consultation and assessment improves outcomes for both mother and baby.
Placental abruption
Placental abruption occurs when the placenta separates from the wall of the uterus before delivery. This is a medical emergency.
Symptoms include:

items: Vaginal bleeding, although bleeding may sometimes be concealed

body.title: Placental abruption is a medical emergency
body.text: Immediate hospital care is essential.
Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome
Severe pain in the upper abdomen, particularly beneath the right ribs, may indicate preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome.
Other symptoms include:

items: Swelling of the face or hands
Nausea or vomiting in late pregnancy

body.title: Urgent assessment is required
body.text: Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome can become life-threatening for both mother and baby.
Other non-obstetrical causes of abdominal pain
Not every episode of abdominal pain is directly related to pregnancy. Women can also develop common medical conditions during pregnancy, including:

Diagnosing these conditions can be more challenging during pregnancy because the growing uterus changes the position of abdominal organs. Healthcare professionals may recommend blood tests, urine tests, or ultrasound to determine the cause safely.
Warning signs that should never be ignored

body.title: Seek urgent medical attention immediately
body.text: Abdominal pain accompanied by any of the following symptoms may indicate a pregnancy emergency that requires immediate medical evaluation.

items: Leakage of fluid from the vagina
Reduced or absent fetal movements after fetal movements have been established
Severe upper abdominal pain with headache or visual changes

body.text: How is abdominal pain during pregnancy diagnosed?
Diagnosing abdominal pain during pregnancy begins with a careful assessment by your healthcare provider.
Your healthcare provider would ask about:

items: The exact location of the pain
Whether the pain is sharp, dull, cramping, or constant
Associated symptoms such as vaginal bleeding, fever, nausea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, contractions, or reduced fetal movements
Your pregnancy history and any previous pregnancy complications

body.text: A physical examination may include checking your abdomen, measuring your blood pressure, assessing your temperature, and listening to your baby’s heartbeat if appropriate for your stage of pregnancy.
Depending on your symptoms, additional investigations may include:
Urine tests
A urine sample can help diagnose:
Blood tests
Blood tests may be performed to look for:

items: Pregnancy hormone (hCG) levels in early pregnancy
Blood group and Rh status if bleeding occurs

body.text: Ultrasound scan
Ultrasound is the preferred imaging test during pregnancy because it does not use radiation.
It may help identify:

items: A normal intrauterine pregnancy and fetal wellbeing
Problems in abdominal organs such as the appendix, gallbladder, liver, kidney, or bladder

body.text: Fetal assessment
Later in pregnancy, your baby’s wellbeing may be assessed using:

items: Fetal heart rate monitoring (cardiotocography or CTG)
Ultrasound assessment of fetal growth and wellbeing

body.text: Occasionally, if ultrasound is inconclusive, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be recommended because it provides excellent images without exposing the fetus to radiation.
Treatment of abdominal pain during pregnancy
Treatment depends entirely on the underlying cause. There is no single treatment suitable for all types of abdominal pain.
Normal pregnancy discomforts
For round ligament pain, Braxton Hicks contractions, or stretching discomfort, treatment usually includes:

items: Wearing supportive maternity clothing if needed

body.text: These symptoms often improve as the body adapts to pregnancy.
Constipation
Constipation can often be managed by:

items: Increasing dietary fibre through fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains
Regular gentle exercise such as walking
Taking pregnancy-safe laxatives if recommended by your healthcare provider

body.text: Urinary tract infection
UTIs require prompt treatment with antibiotics that are considered safe during pregnancy.

Management depends on the size and location of the stone but may include:
Pregnancy complications

Conditions such as ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, severe preeclampsia, HELLP syndrome, or appendicitis require urgent hospital care. Treatment may involve medication, surgery, close monitoring, or early delivery depending on the diagnosis and stage of pregnancy.
Safe home care measures
If your healthcare provider has confirmed that your abdominal pain is not caused by a serious condition, the following measures may help relieve discomfort:

items: Drink enough water throughout the day
Include fibre-rich foods to reduce constipation
Avoid very large meals if they worsen discomfort
Change positions slowly to reduce ligament pain
Use pillows to support your abdomen and back during sleep

body.text: When should you seek emergency medical care?

body.title: Go to your nearest emergency department or contact your maternity unit immediately
body.text: Prompt assessment can help diagnose serious conditions early and improve outcomes for both mother and baby.

items: Fainting or feeling as though you may faint
Leakage of fluid from the vagina
Reduced or absent fetal movements after they have been established
Severe headache with upper abdominal pain or visual disturbances

body.text: Summary

items: Mild abdominal discomfort is common during pregnancy and is often related to normal physical changes.
The causes of abdominal pain vary depending on the stage of pregnancy.
Serious conditions such as ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, preterm labour, appendicitis, and preeclampsia require urgent medical attention.
Persistent, severe, or worsening pain should never be ignored.
Early assessment and appropriate treatment help protect both mother and baby.
If you are unsure whether your symptoms are normal, contact your healthcare provider or maternity unit promptly.

faq.question: Is mild cramping normal during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Mild cramping is common, particularly during early pregnancy and as the uterus grows. However, severe pain, persistent pain, or pain associated with bleeding should always be assessed by a healthcare professional.

faq.question: Can constipation cause severe abdominal pain?
faq.answer: Constipation can cause significant cramping, bloating, and discomfort during pregnancy. However, severe or persistent pain should not automatically be attributed to constipation without medical assessment.

faq.question: Is one-sided abdominal pain always an ectopic pregnancy?
faq.answer: No. One-sided pain may also occur due to other reasons such as round ligament pain, ovarian cysts, the appendix, or other conditions. However, severe one-sided pain in early pregnancy—especially when accompanied by vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, or fainting—requires immediate medical evaluation to exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

faq.question: Can Braxton Hicks contractions be painful?
faq.answer: Braxton Hicks contractions may feel uncomfortable, but they are usually irregular, do not become progressively stronger, and often improve with rest, hydration, or changing position.

faq.question: What does round ligament pain feel like?
faq.answer: Round ligament pain usually causes a sharp, stabbing, or pulling sensation on one or both sides of the lower abdomen or groin. It often occurs suddenly when standing, coughing, sneezing, or changing position.

faq.question: Can abdominal pain be prevented during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Not all causes of abdominal pain can be prevented, but healthy pregnancy habits may reduce the risk of some conditions.
items: Eat a balanced diet rich in fibre
Stay physically active if your healthcare provider advises it is safe
Seek prompt treatment for urinary symptoms
Follow your healthcare provider’s advice regarding existing medical conditions
faq.closing: Although these measures support a healthy pregnancy, they cannot completely prevent complications such as ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, or preeclampsia.

faq.question: Can I take painkillers during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Some painkillers are safe during pregnancy, while others may harm the developing baby. Do not take pain medication without medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider or pharmacist before taking any medication.
